title: The Second and Third Laws of Thermodynamics
lead: The entropy change of a system alone does not decide whether a process is spontaneous; the entropy change of its surroundings must be counted too. The second law of thermodynamics is stated for the universe, and the third law fixes the zero of entropy so that standard entropies can be tabulated and combined for reactions.
objectives: State and explain the second and third laws of thermodynamics
Calculate entropy changes for phase transitions and chemical reactions under standard conditions
summary_html: The second law of thermodynamics states that a spontaneous process increases the entropy of the universe, Suniv > 0. If $\kdSuniv$ < 0, the process is nonspontaneous, and if $\kdSuniv$ = 0, the system is at equilibrium. The third law of thermodynamics establishes the zero for entropy as that of a perfect, pure crystalline solid at 0 K. With only one possible microstate, the entropy is zero. We may compute the standard entropy change for a process by using standard entropy values for the reactants and products involved in the process.
notes: Nothing of the section is left out. Example 16.4 and the summary write “S_univ” without the Δ, Example 16.5’s answer is given in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and Example 16.6’s Check Your Learning sets the state of Ca(OH)₂ upright, all as printed; Table 16.2 gives the values of its cells.

exercises.prompt: Using this information, determine if liquid water will spontaneously freeze at the same temperatures. What can you say about the values of Suniv?

parts.hint: Freezing is the reverse of melting: change the sign of both ΔSsys and qsurr, then add qsurr/T at 263.15 K.
Use the same reversed values with T = 283.15 K.

answer.solution: Entropy is a state function, so ΔSfreezing = −ΔSmelting = −22.1 J/K and qsurr = +6.00 kJ. At −10.00 °C spontaneous, +0.7 J/K; at +10.00 °C nonspontaneous, −0.9 J/K.

exercises.prompt:
Calculate the standard entropy change for the following process:
${\text{H}}_{2}(g)+{\text{C}}_{2}{\text{H}}_{4}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{C}}_{2}{\text{H}}_{6}(g)$

answer.hint: Subtract the standard entropies of H2(g) and C2H4(g) in Table 16.2 from that of C2H6(g).

exercises.prompt:
Calculate the standard entropy change for the following reaction:
$\text{Ca}{(\text{OH})}_{2}(\text{s})\;\longrightarrow \;\text{CaO}(s)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)$

answer.hint: Take the standard entropies of Ca(OH)2(s), CaO(s) and H2O(l) from Appendix G and subtract the reactant’s from the sum of the products’.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between ΔS and ΔS° for a chemical change?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: recall what the degree sign means for a tabulated quantity, the standard conditions of the third-law passage (1 bar, one mole of each substance, usually 298.15 K). Then compare an entropy change measured under whatever conditions the change actually takes place with one computed from standard entropies, and say which of the two Table 16.2 lets you calculate.

parts.hint: Take each standard entropy from Appendix G, multiply it by its coefficient, and subtract the reactants’ sum from the products’.

exercises.prompt: Determine the entropy change for the combustion of gaseous propane, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, under the standard conditions to give gaseous carbon dioxide and water.

answer.hint: Balance C3H8(g) + O2(g) ⟶ CO2(g) + H2O(g), then combine the standard entropies as in Example 16.6.

exercises.prompt:
Using the relevant $S^{\circ}$ values listed in Appendix G, calculate ${\text{Δ}S^{\circ}}_{298}$ for the following changes:
(a) ${\text{N}}_{2}(g)+3{\text{H}}_{2}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;2{\text{NH}}_{3}(g)$
(b) ${\text{N}}_{2}(g)+\;\frac{5}{2}{\text{O}}_{2}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{N}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{5}(g)$

parts.hint: Look up $S^{\circ}$ for N<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>, NH<sub>3</sub>, O<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> in Appendix G and weight each by its coefficient, the fraction 5/2 included.

exercises.prompt:
By calculating ΔSuniv at each temperature, determine if the melting of 1 mole of NaCl(s) is spontaneous at 500 °C and at 700 °C.
${S}_{\text{NaCl}(s)}^{{}^{\circ}}=72.11\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol·K}}\hspace{3em}{S}_{\text{NaCl}(l)}^{{}^{\circ}}=95.06\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol·K}}\hspace{3em}\text{Δ}{H}_{\text{fusion}}^{{}^{\circ}}=\text{27.95 kJ/mol}$
What assumptions are made about the thermodynamic information (entropy and enthalpy values) used to solve this problem?

answer.solution: As ΔSuniv < 0 at each of these temperatures, melting is not spontaneous at either of them. The given values for entropy and enthalpy are for NaCl at 298 K. It is assumed that these do not change significantly at the higher temperatures used in the problem.

exercises.prompt:
Use the standard entropy data in Appendix G to determine the change in entropy for each of the following reactions. All the processes occur at the standard conditions and 25 °C.
(a) $\text{C}(s\text{, graphite})+{\text{O}}_{2}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{CO}}_{2}(g)$
(b) ${\text{O}}_{2}(g)+{\text{N}}_{2}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{2NO}(g)$
(c) $\text{2Cu}(s)+\text{S}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Cu}}_{2}\text{S}(s)$
(d) $\text{CaO}(s)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{Ca}{(\text{OH})}_{2}(s)$
(e) ${\text{Fe}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{3}(s)+\text{3CO}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{2Fe}(s)+{\text{3CO}}_{2}(g)$
(f) ${\text{CaSO}}_{4}\text{·}{\text{2H}}_{2}\text{O}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{CaSO}}_{4}(s)+{\text{2H}}_{2}\text{O}(g)$

parts.hint: Each standard entropy is in Appendix G; multiply by the coefficient and subtract the reactants’ sum from the products’.
